english: And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden. And the Lord God called unto Adam, and said to him, Where are you? And he said to Him, I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself. And He said to him, Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten of the tree whereof I commanded you that you should not eat?
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 114 (Greek, line cut at the scan edge) and p. 116; ANF vol. 2 page unknown

what_it_says: Adam hears "the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden" and answers that he heard the voice; the Greek text itself does not say the voice is the Word.
limits: Unitarian and Arian polemic cites the walking God as corporeal; Theophilus identifies the voice with the Word in 2.22 (see U5-04). Limits: 2.21 by itself does not name the Word; the identification is made in 2.22. The Greek line "περιπατοῦντος ἐν τῷ παραδείσ[ῳ]" is cut at the crop edge and the last letters were read from the page, so re-check on the full page. Page 116 is read in full.

english: but His Word, through whom He made all things, being His power and His wisdom, assuming the person of the Father and Lord of all, went to the garden in the person of God, and conversed with Adam.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 118; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: The Word, being the power and wisdom of God, takes on the prosopon (role, "person") of the Father and Lord of all and speaks with Adam in God's person.
limits: Strongest hard passage for a modalist or "Word as mask" reading: the Word appears "in the person of God". Otto's note (U5-07) cites Humphry for the theatrical sense of prosopon. Limits: Greek prosopon is the theatrical "mask/role" sense here, not the later technical hypostasis. The Greek text printed by Otto has "δύναμις ὢν καὶ σοφία αὐτοῦ" with no brackets. The BKV/Grant text brackets δύναμις and καὶ σοφία as supplements, so the wording is not secure. Nothing here says "Son" or "homoousios".

english: You will say, then, to me: You said that God ought not to be contained in a place, and how do you now say that He walked in Paradise? Hear what I say. The God and Father, indeed, of all cannot be contained, and is not found in a place, for there is no place of His rest;
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 118; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: The Father, as God and Father of all, is incontainable and not located in a place; the Word is the one who goes to a place.
limits: The contrast Father (uncontained) / Word (localised, sent) is the basis of the "binitarian" label: the Word is distinguished from the Father by location and mission. Limits: Not a statement about the Holy Spirit. The printed final letter of ἐστι[ν] was not clear at scan resolution; BKV prints ἐστιν. Clause "ἀχώρητός" is the word the Arian-era texts quote in the Unitarian sense of God's incomprehensibility.

english: But what else is this voice but the Word of God, who is also His Son? Not as the poets and writers of myths talk of the sons of gods begotten from intercourse [with women], but as truth expounds, the Word, that always exists, residing within the heart of God.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 118; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Theophilus says the Word of God, the voice Adam heard, "is also His Son"; this is the only capitalised "Son" in ANF Book II, and the Word is not begotten in the manner of pagan sons of gods.
limits: This is the explicit "Son" statement the brief asks for. Used against Arians it shows a Son who is not a creature; used against Unitarians it shows the Son is the Word. Limits: Only one "Son" in Book II, and it is attached to the endiathetos Word "in the heart of God" (no "homoousios", no "Holy Spirit" in this section). Greek "ἐστιν καὶ υἱὸς" is Otto's reading as printed; BKV agrees. The phrase "who is also His Son" must be read with 2.22 (prophorikos) below, not as a settled Nicene formula.

ref: 2.22 (Otto p. 118; ANF ch. 22; Otto note 10 cites Col. 1:15)
greek: Πρὸ γάρ τι γίνεσθαι τοῦτον εἶχεν σύμβουλον, ἑαυτοῦ νοῦν καὶ φρόνησιν ὄντα. Ὁπότε δὲ ἠθέλησεν ὁ θεὸς ποιῆσαι ὅσα ἐβουλεύσατο, τοῦτον τὸν λόγον ἐγέννησεν προφορικόν, πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως, οὐ κενωθεὶς αὐτὸς τοῦ λόγου, ἀλλὰ λόγον γεννήσας καὶ τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ διὰ παντὸς ὁμιλῶν.

The embedded OCR text layer is garbled for Greek. Cross-checked against the BKV transcription of R. M. Grant (Oxford 1970), which prints editorial supplements in angle brackets.
english: For before anything came into being He had Him as a counsellor, being His own mind and thought. But when God wished to make all that He determined on, He begot this Word, uttered, the first-born of all creation, not Himself being emptied of the Word [Reason], but having begotten Reason, and always conversing with His Reason.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 118; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Before creation the Word is in God as His counsellor (endiathetos), then at God's will he is begotten as uttered (prophorikos), "firstborn of all creation", without God being emptied of the Word.
limits: This is the passage behind the "Word begotten at a point" objection: "ἐγέννησεν προφορικόν" and "πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως" were read by Arians as a creation of the Word. Defence: "not emptied" and "begotten Reason" keep the Word from the divine substance being divided; Otto (note 10) points to Col. 1:15. Limits: The Greek brackets in BKV/Grant mark "πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως" and "δύναμις" as supplements; Otto prints the words without brackets. "προφορικόν" is the technical term the brief lists as a "prolation" word, not a "Triad" word. The Otto printed text has the word split as προφορι-/κόν at a line break. Theophilus does not say "created" for the Word here, but the sentence is open to the Arian reading.

greek: Καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος· πάντα δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἕν. Θεὸς οὖν ὢν ὁ λόγος καὶ ἐκ θεοῦ πεφυκώς, ὁπόταν βούληται ὁ πατὴρ τῶν ὅλων πέμπει αὐτὸν εἴς τινα τόπον, ὃς παραγινόμενος καὶ ἀκούεται καὶ ὁρᾶται, πεμπόμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐν τόπῳ εὑρίσκεται.

english: The Word was God; all things came into existence through Him; and apart from Him not one thing came into existence. The Word, then, being God, and being naturally produced from God, whenever the Father of the universe wills, He sends Him to any place; and He, coming, is both heard and seen, being sent by Him, and is found in a place.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 118 (first sentence) and p. 120 (rest); ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Theophilus quotes John 1:1 and says the Word is God and "naturally produced from God", and that the Father sends him to places where he is heard and seen.
limits: "Θεὸς ... ὁ λόγος" plus "ἐκ θεοῦ πεφυκώς" answers the objection that the sent Word is a creature: he is God by nature (John 1:1). The sending/localising language is what Unitarians cite against him. Limits: The "sending" makes the Word a visible, localised mission; a modern Nicene reading would call this economic (temporal) manifestation. The text does not mention the Spirit. Page 120 is read from the page image; the sentence "καὶ ἐν τόπῳ εὑρίσκεται" is at the end of the chapter.

greek: δύν. ἀν κ. σοφία αὐτοῦ] Cf. c. 10. n. 8. Humphry: „Verbum ἀναλαμβάνων τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ πατρὸς non ita intelligi debent quasi una s. trinitatis persona alteram induceret, vox enim πρόσωπον de personis trinitatis usurpari nondum cooperat, sed, metaphora a theatro sumta, dicit Theophilus filium partes agere patris et illius nomine loqui.“ Cf. Iustin. Apol. I. c. 36 sqq.

english: own translation (marked): Humphry: the phrase "taking up the prosopon of the Father" must not be understood as if one Trinitarian person induced another; the word prosopon was not yet used of Trinitarian persons; taken as a metaphor from the theatre, Theophilus means that the Son plays the Father's part and speaks in his name. Cf. Justin, Apol. I 36 ff.
translator: Otto (editor), quoting Humphry (edition of 1852; the year is from the brief, Otto's note gives no date)
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Otto records that the editor Humphry read the prosopon phrase as a theatrical metaphor and not as a Trinitarian "person"; Humphry also thought the phrase did not mean "one Trinity person induced another".
limits: Standard defence against the modalist/"Word as mask" reading of 2.22; it is an 1850s editorial interpretation, not Theophilus's own statement. Limits: This is a note by an editor, not Theophilus. The Latin wording "Verbum" at the start of the quotation was read at image resolution. Otto's note gives no date for Humphry; the 1852 edition is taken from the brief and was not opened.

greek: Οἱ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι, πνευματοφόροι πνεύματος ἁγίου καὶ προφῆται γινόμενοι, ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐμπνευσθέντες καὶ σοφισθέντες, ἐγένοντο θεοδίδακτοι καὶ ὅσιοι καὶ δίκαιοι. Διὸ καὶ κατηξιώθησαν τὴν ἀντιμισθίαν ταύτην λαβεῖν, ὄργανα θεοῦ γενόμενοι καὶ χωρήσαντες σοφίαν τὴν παρ’ αὐτοῦ, δι’ ἧς σοφίας

english: But men of God carrying in them a holy spirit and becoming prophets, being inspired and made wise by God, became God-taught, and holy, and righteous. Wherefore they were also deemed worthy of receiving this reward, that they should become instruments of God, and contain the wisdom that is from Him, through which wisdom
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 76; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Prophets are men "carrying a holy spirit" (pneumatophoroi, "holy spirit" genitive), inspired and made wise by God, and they "contain the wisdom that is from Him".
limits: "Holy spirit" here is the prophetic inspiration of God. An Arian or Unitarian reading sees the Spirit as an impersonal gift; a Trinitarian reader must add the later doctrine. The Wisdom-in-prophets pairing parallels the Word-Wisdom of 2.10 and 2.22. Limits: Theophilus does not say "Holy Spirit" as a person or as the third member of a Triad here (ANF heading "Holy Ghost" is the translator's). Greek πνεύματος ἁγίου is read from the image; the sentence continues on the following Greek line, which was not fully read.

english: And therefore it is proved that all others have been in error; and that we Christians alone have possessed the truth, inasmuch as we are taught by the Holy Spirit, who spoke in the holy prophets, and foretold all things.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 156 (Latin on p. 157); ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Christians alone have the truth because they are taught "by the holy spirit", who spoke in the holy prophets and foretold all things; the Spirit is the one who speaks (participle λαλήσαντος).
limits: The Spirit is an active speaker in the prophets, which an "objection" reader would take as a mode of God, not a distinct person; a Trinitarian reader can note the personal-looking agency, but Theophilus does not state personhood. Limits: This is the strongest Spirit passage in Book II and it is not a statement of the Holy Spirit's distinct personhood or divinity. Book II ANF has no "Spirit" in chs 19-27 (checked in English text).

ref: 2.24 (Otto p. 124; ANF ch. 24 "The Beauty of Paradise")
greek: διδοὺς αὐτῷ ἀφορμὴν προκοπῆς, ὅπως αὐξάνων καὶ τέλειος γενόμενος, ἵνα δὲ καὶ θεὸς ἀναδειχθείς, οὕτως καὶ εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀναβῇ (μέσος γὰρ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐγένετο, οὔτε θνητὸς ὁλοσχερῶς οὔτε ἀθάνατος τὸ καθόλου, δεκτικὸς δὲ ἑκατέρου· οὕτως καὶ τὸ χωρίον ὁ παράδεισος, ὡς πρὸς καλλονήν, μέσος τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ γέγονεν)

english: God transferred him from the earth, out of which he had been produced, into Paradise, giving him means of advancement, in order that, maturing and becoming perfect, and being even declared a god, he might thus ascend into heaven in possession of immortality. For man had been made a middle nature, neither wholly mortal, nor altogether immortal, but capable of either; so also the place, Paradise, was made in respect of beauty intermediate between earth and heaven.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 124; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: Adam was made a middle nature, neither mortal nor immortal, able to become god and ascend; Paradise is intermediate between earth and heaven.
limits: Context for the "divinisation" theme (man becomes god) that Theophilus uses for the Logos-Son schema; it also shows he thinks of "god" in a derived sense for men. Limits: Not about the Trinity. The phrase "θεὸς ἀναδειχθείς" (declared a god) is a derived use, which opponents use to argue Theophilus's "god" is a creaturely title. Greek read from image.

english: The tree of knowledge itself was good, and its fruit was good. For it was not the tree, as some think, but the disobedience, which had death in it.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 124 (continues p. 126, not read); ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: The tree of knowledge is good in itself; the sin was disobedience, which brought death.
limits: Answers the objection that God forbade knowledge out of envy or that the tree was evil. Not a Trinitarian passage. Limits: Only the opening sentence was read; the Greek continues on page 126, not checked. Theophilus here treats the story as a moral lesson and not as a theological proof.

ref: 2.26-27 (Otto p. 130; ANF ch. 26 end and ch. 27 "The Nature of Man")
greek: Ποῦ εἶ Ἀδάμ; οὐχ ὡς ἀγνοῶν τοῦτο ἐποίει ὁ θεός, ἀλλὰ μακρόθυμος ὢν ἀφορμὴν ἰδίδου μετανοίας καὶ ἐξομολογήσεως. 27. Ἀλλὰ φήσει οὖν τις ἡμῖν· Θνητὸς φύσει ἐγένετο ὁ ἄνθρωπος; Οὐδαμῶς. Τί οὖν ἀθάνατος; Οὐδὲ τοῦτό φαμεν. Ἀλλὰ ἐρεῖ τις· Οὐδὲν οὖν ἐγένετο; Οὐδὲ τοῦτο λέγομεν. Οὔτε οὖν φύσει θνητὸς ἐγένετο οὔτε ἀθάνατος. Εἰ γὰρ ἀθάνατον αὐτὸν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς πεποιήκει, θεὸν αὐτὸν πεποιήκει·
greek_edition: Otto 1861 vol. VIII as reproduced in the 1969 Sändig facsimile; read by the agent from the 300-dpi page image (printed Greek, no brackets). The embedded OCR text layer is garbled for Greek. Cross-checked against the BKV transcription of R. M. Grant (Oxford 1970), which prints editorial supplements in angle brackets.
english: And as to God's calling, and saying, Where are you, Adam? God did this, not as if ignorant of this; but, being long-suffering, He gave him an opportunity of repentance and confession. ... But some one will say to us, Was man made by nature mortal? Certainly not. Was he, then, immortal? Neither do we affirm this. ... He was by nature neither mortal nor immortal. For if He had made him immortal from the beginning, He would have made him God.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)
page: Otto 1861 p. 130; ANF vol. 2 page unknown
edition: Otto, Corpus apologetarum Christianorum vol. VIII (Jena: Mauke, 1861); facsimile Wiesbaden: Sändig, 1969 (Internet Archive item corpusapologeta01moragoog); English: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
what_it_says: God asks "Where are you, Adam?" not from ignorance but to give room for repentance; man was by nature neither mortal nor immortal, since immortal-from-the-start would have made him God.
limits: Answers the objection that God was ignorant (anthropomorphic) and clarifies that the creature was not "immortal by nature", which is the core of the Arian "God alone is unbegotten/immortal" argument. Limits: Not about the Word or Spirit directly. The Greek of 27 continues past "θεὸν αὐτὸν πεποιήκει" on the next page, which was not read. Ellipses in the English mark omitted ANF sentences.

english: But to no one else than to His own Word and wisdom did He say, Let Us make.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, ed. Roberts and Donaldson, rev. A. C. Coxe, 1885)

what_it_says: God says "Let us make" to no one else than His own Word and Wisdom.
limits: Strong "Word and Wisdom as God's co-agents" passage; it supports the "Triad" language of 2.15 (Word and Wisdom as God's own). It does not name the Spirit.
